deep.reconstruction:
The page has two parts.

(A) Reading notes, not mathematics: Herder, 'Ph[ilosophie] u[nd] G[eschichte]', vols. 15, 16, 21, 22 (most likely the section 'Zur Philosophie und Geschichte' of Herder's Sämmtliche Werke). Berkeley, 'A Treatise concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge'. Thibaut, 'Grundriss der allgemeinen Arithmetik oder Algebra' (B. F. Thibaut, Gauss's Göttingen colleague; the printed title of the 1809 book reads '... oder Analysis'). 'Cauchy'. 'Exercitationes Tuong[?]' (an unresolved title).

(B) 'Ellipsograph generalisirt' (generalized ellipsograph, i.e. a generalized trammel of Archimedes).

Set-up as I read the figure (my reading):
- A rigid rod ac has end a sliding on a horizontal line and end c sliding on a vertical line. The two lines meet at O, the lower-right corner of the figure.
- b is the point of ac with ab = bc = r (the midpoint).
- d is a point rigidly attached to the rod at distance bd = s. In the figure d is off the line ac, joined to b, a and c.

Step 1 (implicit, mine). Since angle aOc is a right angle, b is the circumcentre of triangle aOc, so Ob = ab = r. Hence b moves on a circle of radius r about O. With O as origin and complex coordinates, b = r e^{i phi}, where phi is the angle of Ob.
- Then a = 2r cos(phi) (on the horizontal axis) and c = 2i r sin(phi) (on the vertical axis).
- So c - a = -2r e^{-i phi}. The direction of the rod is therefore pi - phi: as phi increases, the rod turns by -phi.

Step 2. Because d is fixed to the rod, the vector bd keeps a constant angle to the rod. So bd = s e^{i(alpha - phi)} for a constant alpha, and
d = r e^{i phi} + s e^{i(alpha - phi)}.
This is Gauss's statement: d's motion is composed of two opposite circular motions with radii ab and bd.

Step 3 (implicit, mine). Put psi = phi - alpha/2 and rotate the frame by alpha/2:
d e^{-i alpha/2} = r e^{i psi} + s e^{-i psi} = (r+s) cos(psi) + i (r-s) sin(psi).
This is an ellipse with semi-axes r+s = ab+bd and |r-s| = ab-bd, as Gauss writes. Its axes are inclined at alpha/2 to the guide lines, and it is centred at O.

The point of the generalization: not only points on the line ac, but every point of the plane rigidly carried by the rod traces an ellipse.
errors: No real error. Minor imprecision: the second semi-axis is |ab - bd|; Gauss's 'ab - bd' tacitly assumes ab > bd.
Unstated: if d is not on line ac, the ellipse's axes are rotated by alpha/2 relative to the guide lines. If s = r the ellipse degenerates to a segment, the classical straight-line case.

results.what: In the trammel (Cardan) motion of a rod whose ends slide on two perpendicular lines, any point rigidly attached to the rod at distance bd from the midpoint b traces an ellipse with semi-axes ab+bd and |ab-bd|. The proof writes the motion as the sum of two equal-speed, opposite rotations.
results.modern_name: Elliptic trammel / Cardan motion (every point of the moving plane describes an ellipse); ellipse as the sum of two counter-rotating circular motions
results.usually_credited_to: Trammel of Archimedes (antiquity); Proclus; Cardano; de La Hire (c. 1706) for the moving-plane/rolling-circle description; ellipse as the sum of opposite rotations is classical (epicyclic tradition)

results.what: Reading list (Herder, Berkeley, Thibaut, Cauchy, an unidentified 'Exercitationes').

deep.surprise_reason: This is an elegant, correct, short derivation of a classical kinematic fact (the Cardan/trammel motion) that was well known before Gauss. It is interesting mainly as evidence of his interest in mechanisms and of his reading, not as a new result.

The parametrized point satisfies the ellipse equation x^2/(r+s)^2 + y^2/(r-s)^2 = 1.
